prompt: Who is an incident record mainly written for?

choices.text: The manager, as proof the work was done
choices.why: Proof of work is a side effect; the record's value is to whoever meets the fault again.

choices.text: Whoever meets the same fault next time
choices.why: Right. The second search starts from the answer instead of from the cable.

choices.text: The person who fixed it, as a diary
choices.why: They are the one reader who least needs it, until they forget.

choices.text: The users, so they stop reporting it
choices.why: Users want to know it was understood, but they are not who searches the record.

prompt: Why is a record written a week after the incident unreliable?
hint: What does memory do with a week?

choices.text: It is too late to count towards the SLA
choices.why: An SLA counts downtime from the timeline, whenever the record is written.

choices.text: The fix will have been undone by then
choices.why: Nothing undoes a fix on a timetable; the problem is the writer, not the fix.

choices.text: Memory tidies it and drops the failures
choices.why: Right. The record starts as timed notes during the incident, and is tidied afterwards.

choices.text: The people affected have forgotten the symptom
choices.why: The symptom was measured, and the measurement does not fade.

prompt: A year later hq gets a second WireGuard tunnel, wg1, for people working from home. Why does lesson 21's record matter to it?
hint: Read the fix's rules again: which interface do they name?

choices.text: The rule still drops the message, and the clamping names wg0 only
choices.why: Right. wg1 meets the same black hole unless it gets its own clamping, or the rule is narrowed.

choices.text: WireGuard tunnels lose MTU as they age
choices.why: An MTU is a setting; it does not wear out.

choices.text: The clamping rules expire after a year
choices.why: nftables rules stay until somebody removes them.

choices.text: Home connections send smaller packets
choices.why: A home laptop sends full-size packets like any other machine on Ethernet.

prompt: Which of these is a symptom, in the sense the record uses?

choices.text: The VPN between the offices is broken
choices.why: That is a first theory dressed as a fact.

choices.text: The tunnel's MTU is set wrong on hq
choices.why: That is a hypothesis, and it needs a test.

choices.text: 0 bytes for big.bin after 8002 ms
choices.why: Right. What was seen, measured, with no cause attached.

choices.text: The firewall is blocking large downloads
choices.why: A cause again, and in this case a wrong one: it blocked ICMP, not downloads.

prompt: Why does the record keep the hypotheses that turned out wrong?

choices.text: So nobody spends time testing them again
choices.why: Right. A refuted hypothesis is a result, often the most useful one.

choices.text: Because an audit requires every step to be listed
choices.why: Some audits do, but the reason here is the next diagnosis, not the audit.

choices.text: To show how hard the engineer worked
choices.why: Effort is not the point; ruled-out causes are.

choices.text: A wrong hypothesis will be right the next time
choices.why: It might or might not; the record keeps it because it was tested, not as a prediction.

prompt: Why is a test's output pasted into the record rather than summarised?

choices.text: Pasting is faster during an incident
choices.why: It often is, but that is not what makes it right.

choices.text: A summary cannot be searched later
choices.why: A summary can be searched; what it loses is the detail nobody knew would matter.

choices.text: Nobody knows yet which detail will matter
choices.why: Right. 'The big ping failed' loses the missing +1 errors, which was the clue.

choices.text: The tools' output cannot be shortened safely
choices.why: Output can be cut to whole commands; the point is not to reword what they printed.

prompt: Match each field of the record to lesson 21's entry.
hint: The symptom has no cause in it.

pairs.right: Packets over the tunnel's MTU are lost

prompt: Put the record's fields in the order they are filled in.
trap: A test comes after the hypothesis it is meant to refute, and a fix after a result that confirmed something.

hint: Hours and minutes, relative to UTC.

choices.text: The clock is three hours ahead of UTC
choices.why: The sign is the other way: minus means behind, so UTC is 21:17:16.

choices.text: Local time is UTC minus three hours
choices.why: Right. The lab's clock runs on America/Sao_Paulo.

choices.text: An offset of 300 seconds from UTC
choices.why: It is hours and minutes, 03:00, not seconds.

choices.text: That summer time was in force that day
choices.why: An offset is just the difference; São Paulo has had no summer time since 2019.

prompt: The mtr report started at 18:17:16 at `-03:00`. What hour is that in UTC?
Every time in a record carries its ___ from UTC, or it cannot be lined up with logs written in another zone.
A firewall log without offsets shows a change at 13:58, and the ticket system, in UTC, shows the first failed download at 16:59. The firewall runs on São Paulo time. What do you conclude?

choices.text: They are three hours apart and unrelated
choices.why: Taken at face value they are; converted, they are not.

choices.text: The change came a minute before
choices.why: Right. 13:58 at -03:00 is 16:58 UTC, a minute before 16:59.

choices.text: The failure came first, so the change cannot be the cause
choices.why: That reads 16:59 as local time; it is UTC.

choices.text: The firewall's clock is wrong by three hours
choices.why: It is right in its own zone; the log just did not say which.

prompt: What does a blameless post-mortem ask about the hardening rule?

choices.text: Who added it, and why they were careless
choices.why: That teaches people to hide the next mistake.

choices.text: What let it in unnoticed
choices.why: Right. What made it easy to add and hard to see changes the process, so the next such rule is caught.

choices.text: Whether hardening rules should be banned
choices.why: Hardening is still right; this rule needed narrowing, not banning.

choices.text: Whether the engineer should lose firewall access
choices.why: Punishment removes the person most likely to spot the next one.

prompt: Which action item is complete as written?
hint: An owner, a date and a test.

choices.text: Improve firewall hygiene across the network
choices.why: No owner, no date, and nothing that says when it is done.

choices.text: The network team will look into the MTU issues this quarter
choices.why: A team is not one owner, and 'look into' has no test for done.

choices.text: Ana; Friday; the 1400 ping prints Frag needed
choices.why: Right. Ana narrows the rule: one owner, a date, and a test anybody can run.

choices.text: Stop dropping ICMP on the routers
choices.why: A slogan with no owner or date, and wrong as stated: some ICMP should be dropped.

prompt: Which of these does an action item need? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: One owner
choices.why: Right: an action item without an owner is a wish.

choices.text: A test that says it is done
choices.why: Right: otherwise done is whatever somebody says it is.

choices.text: The name of whoever caused the incident
choices.why: That is blame, and it fixes nothing.

choices.text: A date
choices.why: Right: without one, it is done after the fault comes back.

prompt: Why does the record write 'the hardening rule drops type 3 messages on hq's output' instead of naming who wrote the rule?
hint: Who has to read it and act on it?

choices.text: Because the author bears no responsibility for it
choices.why: Blameless is not ownerless: someone still owns the fix.

choices.text: It names what to fix, in words its author agrees with
choices.why: Right. The sentence points at the mechanism, and the person who wrote the rule is free to fix it without defending themselves.

choices.text: Because the law requires post-mortems to be anonymous
choices.why: No law is involved; it is a choice about what makes people report mistakes.

choices.text: To keep the record short
choices.why: A name is shorter than the sentence; length is not the reason.

prompt: The write-up gives the cause as two conditions together. Which two?

choices.text: A wrong gateway and a stopped web server
choices.why: Those were two other faults of lesson 21, staged separately.

choices.text: wg0's 1420 MTU, and hq dropping its own frag-needed message
choices.why: Right. The first is normal for a tunnel; the second makes it a black hole.

choices.text: ICMP rate limiting and a lossy uplink
choices.why: Those belong to lesson 22; nothing was lost at random here.

choices.text: A WireGuard key mismatch and a short curl timeout
choices.why: The small page crossed the tunnel, so the keys matched; and a longer timeout would still get 0 bytes.

prompt: Why is lesson 21's timeline an order with no times?

choices.text: Times would reveal where the lab is
choices.why: The captures already say TZ=America/Sao_Paulo; nothing was being hidden.

choices.text: It all happened too fast to time
choices.why: Speed is no reason: a clock can stamp a millisecond.

choices.text: Nobody noted the clock as it happened
choices.why: Right. The transcripts kept the order and no clock, and nothing recovers it now.

choices.text: Records list the order, not the times
choices.why: A record wants times with offsets; this one simply could not have them.

prompt: Hypothesis 1 of the write-up was refuted by a single curl of the small page. Why was that one command worth so much?
hint: What must work for 16 bytes to arrive?

choices.text: It measured the tunnel's MTU directly
choices.why: The MTU came from ping and ip link; the page says nothing about size.

choices.text: It proved the name, route, tunnel and server in one go
choices.why: Right. A 200 needs all four working, so four suspects left the list together.

choices.text: It exposed the hardening rule
choices.why: The rule came from nft list ruleset, three steps later.

choices.text: It was the first test run from the till
choices.why: Being first is not what made it worth so much; big.bin was fetched from the till right after.

prompt: Another company's record reads: 'Cause: human error. Action: be more careful.' What is wrong with it?

choices.text: It is too short to be taken seriously
choices.why: A short record can be excellent; this one is empty, not short.

choices.text: It should say which human
choices.why: Naming the person makes it worse, not better.

choices.text: No mechanism, and no testable action
choices.why: Right. 'Human error' is where the questions start, and 'be careful' has no owner, date or test.

choices.text: It blames a person instead of a team
choices.why: Blaming a team is still blame; the record needs the mechanism that let the mistake through.

prompt: A log line written in UTC says `21:17:40Z`. What hour is that on the lab's clock, at `-03:00`?
A post-mortem that looks for what made a mistake easy, rather than for somebody to punish, is called ___.
